definition: Contextualize means to place something within its surrounding circumstances so it can be understood.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word contextualize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know contextualize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The pediatrician contextualized the growth chart before the parents could worry: their daughter was small, but exactly as small as she had always been.
A caption is far weaker than contextualize — a date and a name beneath a photo, where contextualizing builds the whole surrounding picture.
Recreate goes further than contextualize: instead of explaining a thing's surroundings, you rebuild them entirely, room by room or scene by scene.

Situate places a thing in its time and place — a treaty in 1648, a speech on a courthouse step — and stops there. Contextualize keeps going: it builds the surrounding circumstances that make the thing intelligible, the whole picture rather than just the pin on the map.

Frame sets the border around how something is seen, and the border can carry a slant — the same layoff framed as trimming fat or as gutting a team. Contextualize is more neutral and more complete: it supplies the surrounding circumstances rather than an angle on them.

Contextualize is the precise verb because the number is not being corrected or translated — it is being surrounded with the circumstances that let it make sense.
Explain would be vaguer; situate would only park it in 1955; contextualize builds the whole frame.
Contextualize belongs to classrooms, museums, and journalism — building the surroundings that make a fact intelligible.
Unlike construe, its neighbor in this unit, which works out what the words themselves mean, contextualize supplies what sits around them.

The headline said shark encounters off the county's beaches had doubled in a single summer.
Town forums lit up; a petition demanded nets.
The number was true, and on its own it was terrifying.
Then the marine institute published a short note that did nothing but contextualize the figure.
Encounters had gone from two to four -- in a season when beach visits had tripled after the new ferry opened, and when 'encounter' included any sighting within a hundred yards.
Warmer currents had also shifted the sardine run, which sharks follow, closer to shore for a few weeks.
Nothing in the note said the number was wrong.
It said the number had been alone -- and that, surrounded by its circumstances, it stopped meaning what the headline implied.
